paragraphs.title: The Greatness and Beauty of Jerusalem

answers: Great and greatly to be praised
Weak and forgotten
Silent and hidden
easy.explanation: The passage begins, “Great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised.”
easy.q: How is the LORD described at the beginning of the passage?

answers: Beautiful and the joy of the whole earth
Empty and ruined
Small and unnoticed
easy.explanation: Mount Zion is called “Beautiful for situation, the joy of the whole earth.”

answers: God as a refuge
The strength of the kings
The ships of Tarshish
easy.explanation: The verse says, “God is known in her palaces for a refuge.”
easy.q: What is known in the city’s palaces?

answers: The holy city associated with God’s presence
A city ruled only by earthly kings
A seaport for merchants
medium.explanation: The passage presents the city as belonging to God and connected with His holiness.
medium.q: What does “the city of our God” refer to in this passage?

answers: That Zion is a source of joy for all the earth
That Zion is hidden from the earth
That Zion is feared by every nation
medium.explanation: The phrase portrays Zion as bringing joy broadly, not merely to one group.
medium.q: What does the phrase “the joy of the whole earth” communicate?

answers: God’s greatness, Zion’s beauty, and God’s refuge
Kings’ warfare, ships’ voyages, and exile
Judgment, mourning, and national defeat
medium.explanation: The verses move from praise of God to the beauty of Zion and God’s protection in the city.
medium.q: Which sequence best summarizes these verses?

answers: They show a beautiful city whose security comes from God
They show that the city depends only on its palaces
They show that the city is unrelated to God
challenge.explanation: The city is both beautiful and secure because God is known there as a refuge.
challenge.q: How do Zion’s beauty and God’s refuge work together in the passage?

answers: The city’s apparent strength points to God as its true protection
The palaces are empty and abandoned
The kings provide the city’s only defense
challenge.explanation: The wording directs attention from the buildings themselves to God as the source of safety.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from God being known in the palaces “for a refuge”?

answers: The mountain of his holiness and the city of the great King
The east wind and the ships of Tarshish
The generation following and death
challenge.explanation: These phrases identify Zion with holiness and with the great King.
challenge.q: Which combination most strongly emphasizes Jerusalem’s special status?

paragraphs.title: Kings Overwhelmed by the City’s Power

answers: The kings
The daughters of Judah
The priests
easy.explanation: The verse says, “the kings were assembled, they passed by together.”
easy.q: Who were assembled and passed by together?

answers: They marvelled, were troubled, and hastened away
They rejoiced and stayed there
They built new palaces
easy.explanation: They saw the city, marvelled, became troubled, and hurried away.
easy.q: How did the kings react when they saw the city?

answers: The pain of a woman in travail
The warmth of the sun
The joy of a feast
easy.explanation: Their fear is described as “pain, as of a woman in travail.”
easy.q: What was the kings’ fear compared to?

answers: They hurried away
They quietly rested
They proudly entered
medium.explanation: The phrase means that the frightened kings quickly departed.
medium.q: What does “hasted away” mean in this context?

answers: They were distressed and alarmed
They were peaceful and satisfied
They were generous and cheerful
medium.explanation: In this context, “troubled” describes their distress and fear.
medium.q: What does the word “troubled” communicate about the kings?

answers: It breaks the ships, illustrating great destructive power
It guides the ships safely into harbor
It fills the ships with treasure
medium.explanation: The east wind is pictured as powerful enough to break the ships of Tarshish.
medium.q: How does the east wind relate to the ships of Tarshish?

answers: It presents them as a group that witnesses the city and responds with fear
It shows that only one king saw the city
It indicates that they came to celebrate their ships
challenge.explanation: Their united movement makes their shared astonishment and fear more striking.
challenge.q: Why does the phrase “they passed by together” strengthen the description of the kings’ reaction?

answers: Both images convey sudden and overwhelming power
Both images describe peaceful celebration
Both images concern the city’s trade
challenge.explanation: The frightened kings and the shattered ships are parallel pictures of overwhelming force.
challenge.q: What connection exists between the kings’ trouble and the breaking ships?

answers: It makes the kings’ fear vivid by comparing it with a destructive storm
It explains how Tarshish was founded
It describes ordinary commerce in Jerusalem
challenge.explanation: The image gives the reader a strong picture of danger and irresistible power.
challenge.q: What is the purpose of the image of ships being broken?

paragraphs.title: What Was Heard Becomes Seen and Assured

answers: What they had heard was what they saw
What they had heard was completely false
They were unable to see the city
easy.explanation: The passage says, “As we have heard, so have we seen.”
easy.q: What did the visitors discover about what they had heard?

answers: The city of the LORD of hosts and the city of our God
The city of the kings
The city of the ships
easy.explanation: The verse uses both “the city of the LORD of hosts” and “the city of our God.”
easy.q: How is Jerusalem identified in the passage?

answers: God’s judgments
The kings’ fear
The east wind
easy.explanation: The passage says they should be glad “because of thy judgments.”
easy.q: What causes mount Zion and the daughters of Judah to rejoice?

answers: Their experience confirmed what they had previously heard
The city appeared smaller than its reputation
They refused to believe the report
medium.explanation: The phrase means that what they saw matched the report they had received.
medium.q: What does “As we have heard, so have we seen” mean?

answers: God’s faithful mercy is recognized in His sanctuary
The kings have built a new temple
The temple has been emptied of worship
medium.explanation: The worshippers reflect on God’s loyal mercy within His temple.
medium.q: What is meant by “thy lovingkindness” in the midst of the temple?

answers: His praise reaches the ends of the earth according to His name
His praise remains only inside the temple
His praise belongs only to earthly kings
medium.explanation: The verse says, “According to thy name, O God, so is thy praise unto the ends of the earth.”
medium.q: How are God’s name and praise related?

answers: Hearing, seeing, recognizing mercy and righteousness, and rejoicing
Fear, battle, exile, and rebuilding
Ships, towers, trade, and inheritance
challenge.explanation: The passage moves from confirmed testimony to reflection on God’s mercy, righteousness, judgments, and joy.
challenge.q: Which sequence best describes the movement of thought in these verses?

answers: The city’s lasting stability is connected with God’s purpose
The city will exist only briefly
The city depends entirely on human rulers
challenge.explanation: The verse attributes the city’s enduring establishment to God.
challenge.q: What does the statement that God will establish the city “for ever” suggest?

answers: Joy arises from recognizing God’s righteous rule and judgments
Judgment is presented only as a cause of despair
The passage separates joy completely from justice
challenge.explanation: The verses connect gladness with God’s righteous judgments and faithful rule.
challenge.q: How do righteousness, judgments, and rejoicing fit together?

paragraphs.title: Examining the City and Passing on Its Memory

answers: Walk about it and go round about it
Leave it immediately
Sail away from it
easy.explanation: The verse says, “Walk about Zion, and go round about her.”
easy.q: What are the people told to do around Zion?

answers: The towers, bulwarks, and palaces
The ships and foreign kings
The storms and battlefields
easy.explanation: They are told to tell the towers, mark the bulwarks, and consider the palaces.
easy.q: What are they told to tell and consider?

answers: The generation following
Only the kings
Only the priests
easy.explanation: The purpose is “that ye may tell it to the generation following.”
easy.q: To whom should they tell what they have seen?

answers: So they can preserve and communicate the city’s greatness to the next generation
So they can search for ships
So they can frighten the daughters of Judah
medium.explanation: Careful observation leads to testimony for those who come afterward.
medium.q: Why are the people told to examine the towers, bulwarks, and palaces?

answers: The next generation to whom the testimony will be passed
The kings who previously visited the city
The generation that built the ships
medium.explanation: The phrase refers to future generations who will receive the account.

answers: He is our God for ever and will be our guide even unto death
He guides only earthly kings
He guides only within the city walls
medium.explanation: The final verse presents God as the eternal God and guide of His people.
medium.q: What does the final verse emphasize about God?

answers: Seeing its features gives the people something concrete to teach future generations
Remembering the city makes its features unimportant
The passage says there is no connection between seeing and telling
challenge.explanation: The people inspect the city so they can accurately tell the next generation about it.
challenge.q: How are examining the city and preserving its memory connected?

answers: The passage moves from observing towers and palaces to recognizing God’s eternal guidance
The passage moves from memory to warfare
The passage moves from ships to commerce
challenge.explanation: The physical city leads to the larger truth that God guides His people forever.
challenge.q: What is the major transition from the city’s structures to the final verse?

answers: God’s enduring and eternal sovereignty
A specific location in the city
A temporary experience of fear
challenge.explanation: The repeated phrase stresses the everlasting nature of God’s rule and care.
challenge.q: What does the phrase “for ever and ever” emphasize?
